newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Republicans propose mastectomy coverage law.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Republicans propose mastectomy coverage law.

text.p: In a move to stop health insurance companies from rushing women out of hospitals after mastectomies, three New York lawmakers on Monday proposed a law to improve care for those recovering from breast cancer.

The law would require insurance carriers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care for mastectomies and lymph node dissection for the treatment of breast cancer and guarantee coverage of reconstructive surgery for mastectomy patients.

The "Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act of 1997" would also guarantee coverage of second opinions for all forms of cancer and ensure that doctors were not penalised by Health Maintenance Organisations (HMOs) for recommending such care or an extended hospital stay.

Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, Representative Susan Molinari and Representative Sue Kelly, all Republicans, said women were too often discharged early from hospitals after "drive-by" or "drive-in" mastectomies because HMOs wanted to keep down costs.

They underlined the importance of reconstructive surgery because studies show that fear of losing a breast is a leading reason why women do not take part in early breast cancer detection tests. Although carriers cover surgery for patients disfigured in car accidents or tumour removal, they do not always cover reconstructive surgery after a mastectomy.

"The length of stay should be decided by the patient in conjunction with sound medical advice given by her physician, not some bean counter at some insurance company who decides that we can move patients in and out within 48 hours or 24 hours," D'Amato told a news conference.
In recent years, he has been involved in raising money for more research on breast cancer after studies showed a high incidence of the disease on Long Island, New York.

"This is a great day for us but unfortunately for many victims of breast cancer and all cancer it's too late," said Jerry Barish, a breast cancer survivor and president of a New York support group. "We are appalled to think that our insurance companies are playing God with our lives, telling us the morning after surgery that we're going to be fine and we should go home."
Kelly said 180,000 women were diagonosed with breast cancer in 1996 nationwide and 44,300 were expected to die.
D'Amato predicted "vast" bipartisan support for the bill, which will be introduced in the Senate and the House on the first day of the 105th Congress in January.
